questions.prompt: What first distinction does Chapter 10 use to measure strength?
choices: Whether the prince rules through fear or love
Whether the prince can support himself with his own resources or needs the assistance of others
Whether the prince inherited the state or conquered it

explanation.gentle: The chapter opens by asking whether the prince can stand on his own resources in need.
explanation.direct: Machiavelli measures strength by self-support versus dependency before he discusses anything else.
explanation.competitive: The first test is whether the regime owns its survival or rents it.

questions.prompt: What marks the weaker condition in Chapter 10?
choices: Being forced to defend oneself by sheltering behind walls
Having too much money and too few men
Being loved by the people more than feared

explanation.gentle: The weaker case is the prince who cannot meet the enemy in the field and must shelter behind walls.
explanation.direct: Machiavelli distinguishes open-field capacity from defensive survival inside the town.
explanation.competitive: Once the ruler cannot show himself in the field, the whole strategic condition changes.

questions.prompt: Why does Machiavelli tell the wall-backed prince not to defend the whole country?
choices: Because visible countryside loss never matters politically
Because country people always prefer foreign rule
Because scattered defence wastes force that should secure the one place that can truly hold

explanation.gentle: He wants the prince to defend the town that can really hold rather than spread strength thinly everywhere.
explanation.direct: The point is concentration. The weaker prince should not perform open-field breadth he cannot sustain.
explanation.competitive: Trying to save every edge is how the regime bleeds away the only force it actually had.

questions.prompt: Inez cannot protect every site in her network. According to Chapter 10, what is the better move?
choices: Concentrate on the defendable hub and keep the staff there from feeling abandoned
Promise to save all six sites so morale stays high
Wait for outside partners to decide which site matters

explanation.gentle: Chapter 10 favors defending the core that can truly hold.
explanation.direct: Inez should match defended ground to real capacity and keep the people inside that core supported.
explanation.competitive: The honest hub is stronger than six fake perimeters.

questions.prompt: What did Corbin's postmortem show about the fabrication lab cage?
choices: It survived because closure looked tedious and the room was prepared to keep functioning
It survived because students never noticed the threat
It survived because machines alone are more persuasive than people

explanation.gentle: The room held because preparation made it look hard to shut down cleanly.
explanation.direct: Supplies, routines, and visible work mattered as much as the equipment itself.
explanation.competitive: The lab looked ready to outlast the attack, and that changed the whole fight.

questions.prompt: What lesson does June's storm dialogue bring out?
choices: That every perimeter deserves equal defence until the last minute
That honest concentration on what can hold is wiser than trying to save every exposed edge
That outside damage should never be accepted under any conditions

explanation.gentle: June learns that the defendable core matters more than a symbolic full rescue.
explanation.direct: Chapter 10 turns prudence into honest concentration rather than sprawl.
explanation.competitive: The fake full defence burns the strength needed for the place that could have held.

questions.prompt: Why does Machiavelli care whether the prince is hated by his people?
choices: Because hatred makes fortification a weaker defence from the inside
Because hatred always prevents the prince from storing provisions
Because hatred matters only to open-field armies

explanation.gentle: A city does not count as strong in the same way if the people inside hate the ruler.
explanation.direct: Anti-odium is part of the defensive condition, not a separate moral lecture.
explanation.competitive: The inner front can fail long before the outer wall is breached.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the German cities example?
choices: That any free city can ignore neighboring powers forever
That strong walls by themselves automatically make citizens loyal
That visible difficulty grows out of fortification joined to stores, work, exercises, and ordinances

explanation.gentle: The example shows a city prepared to last, not merely enclosed by walls.
explanation.direct: Machiavelli uses Germany to display organized endurance rather than hardware alone.
explanation.competitive: Attack looks ugly when the whole city already knows how to keep functioning under pressure.

questions.prompt: How does Machiavelli answer the objection that burnt property outside the walls will make citizens forget their prince?
choices: He says the prince should deny that any real damage occurred
He says a powerful prince can keep minds steady through hope, fear of the enemy, practical support, and adroit handling of the bold
He says citizens never care about their property when war begins

explanation.gentle: He does not deny the pain. He says the prince must still guide minds and support the citizens through it.
explanation.direct: Hope, fear of enemy cruelty, and visible defence can keep loss from turning into immediate political collapse.
explanation.competitive: The regime holds when the prince carries the siege with the people instead of leaving them alone in the damage.

questions.prompt: If a prince cannot meet the enemy in the field, what should he secure first according to Chapter 10?
choices: Every stretch of the countryside before the town itself
A fortified and provisioned city whose people do not hate him
A promise that outside allies will eventually rescue him

explanation.gentle: The chapter's threshold is the defended town, not the whole country and not borrowed rescue.
explanation.direct: Machiavelli tells the weaker prince to secure the holdable core and the people's temper inside it.
explanation.competitive: Real strength begins where the regime can still stand on its own after the perimeter is gone.
